Chapter 1: The Search for Meaning Beyond the Surface
There’s this moment that comes to so many of us who spend our days surrounded by images—whether you’re painting, teaching, or just really looking at the world—when everything starts to feel a little thin. Like, the surface of things, no matter how beautifully rendered or admired, somehow loses its grip. And in that gentle pause, a question bubbles up: is art really just what you see on the surface, or is there something more?
Funny enough, this question doesn’t usually show up in grand museums. It sneaks in during the smallest, most ordinary moments of creativity. Picture someone—a friend, maybe, or a teacher—who’s always loved painting landscapes. For years, they’ve chased the shimmer of light on water, that perfect curve of a hill, the exact blue of a summer sky. Their skill grows, people praise their work... but after a while, restlessness creeps in. The paintings, though lovely, start to feel like echoes of something just out of reach.
That feeling? It can be tricky to name. Some folks try to shake it off by perfecting their technique, adding more details, or searching for new subjects. Others dive into the art of the past, hoping the old masters might offer some answers. Yet, the sense sticks around—art, when it’s really alive, seems to promise more than just a perfect copy of the world. It hints at a secret layer, a kind of inner life you can’t measure or pin down.
And here’s the thing: this longing for something beyond the obvious isn’t just a personal itch. It’s part of art’s entire history. Over centuries, artists have shifted from strict imitation of nature to wild experiments with color, form, and pure abstraction. Every one of those leaps has been driven by the desire to reach past the material world and touch something essential—something, well, spiritual.
Now, when you hear “spiritual,” maybe you think of religion or mysticism. But in art, it’s broader than that. It’s about what happens inside—the inner experience, that emotional resonance, the feeling of connection when a work of art speaks to your soul, not just your senses. This spiritual dimension isn’t about any single faith or philosophy. It’s universal. It’s about our deep need to find meaning, to discover beauty that moves both the heart and the mind.
Back in the early twentieth century, when the world was changing fast and old certainties were falling away, this search for a spiritual meaning in art suddenly felt more urgent. With photography and mass production on the rise, it was clear that just representing what we see wasn’t enough anymore. Artists started asking themselves: if a camera can record the look of things in an instant, what’s left for us as painters, sculptors, creators? For many, the answer was to look inward—to explore feeling, intuition, imagination.
Sure, there was resistance. Plenty of people still believed that art’s highest calling was to mirror reality, to please the eye and educate the mind. But others sensed that true art had to go further. It needed to express the artist’s inner world—the invisible forces shaping our thoughts and emotions. It needed to awaken something in the viewer that words just can’t touch.
That’s where abstraction started to take root. It wasn’t about rejecting the visible world, but about reaching for the spiritual essence behind what we see. By letting go of the need to depict objects or scenes, artists could focus on pure color, line, and form—creating works that speak straight to the soul, skipping over the intellect, and landing somewhere deeper.
The journey from the material to the spiritual isn’t simple. It’s messy, uncertain, full of experiments—and sometimes, failures. But for those who keep going, the rewards are profound. Art becomes more than just a craft or a job. It turns into a calling—a way to explore the mysteries of being alive, and to share those discoveries with others.
